w:r.w:t: System and Method for Gas-Hazard Classification and Mitigation Using Fan Coast-Down Aerodynamic Densitometry with Thermodynamic-Residual Compensation and Chemoresistive Disambiguation

This invention belongs to the fields of embedded instrumentation, physical gas sensing and environmental safety control. It describes an apparatus and a method in which a small axial fan, normally used only as an actuator, is operated as a measuring element. The fan is spun up and its supply is interrupted. The time taken for each revolution during the ensuing free coast-down is recorded, and the resulting speed-decay record is fitted to a rotor-dynamics model that separates the speed-independent and viscous friction losses of the bearing from the aerodynamic loss of the blades. The aerodynamic coefficient is proportional to the density of the surrounding gas and is converted into a density estimate. That estimate is compared with the density that dry and humid air would have at the prevailing temperature, relative humidity and pressure, measured by a co-located environmental sensor. The remaining difference, the thermodynamic density residual, isolates the contribution of a foreign gas of molecular mass different from that of air. A metal-oxide chemoresistive (MQ-series) sensor supplies a second, physically independent signal. The pair of signals is used to assign the atmosphere to one of five hazard classes and to select a mitigation action appropriate to that class, including suppression of fan energisation and choice of a high or low vent path when a combustible gas is indicated.

Low-cost gas monitoring in rooms, cabinets, cylinder stores and small workshops relies almost entirely on metal-oxide chemoresistive sensors. Such sensors respond to reducing and combustible gases and to organic vapours, and they are strongly affected by temperature and humidity, but they give little or no response to inert asphyxiants such as carbon dioxide at percent-level concentration or helium. They also cannot say whether a detected gas is lighter or heavier than air, which determines where it accumulates and therefore where it must be vented. Two consequences follow. An asphyxiant leak can progress without any response from the installed detector. A combustible leak may be answered by energising an exhaust fan, which is itself a potential ignition source, and by venting from the wrong height. A physical measurement of gas density, compensated for the ordinary variation of air density with the weather, supplies exactly the two pieces of information the chemoresistive sensor lacks. It indicates that the composition of the air has changed, and it gives the sign of the change, which is heavier or lighter than air. The present invention obtains that measurement from a fan that the protection system requires in any case.
2.1 Technical Problem Addressed by the Invention

Metal-oxide chemoresistive gas sensors are not responsive to inert asphyxiants such as carbon dioxide and helium at the percent-level concentrations relevant to oxygen displacement, so a sensor of this kind alone cannot detect that class of hazard.

A chemoresistive response does not indicate whether the gas responsible is lighter or heavier than air, so it cannot by itself choose between a high and a low ventilation path. Nor can it separate a combustible gas from a benign organic vapour that produces a comparable resistance change.

The density of ambient air changes by several per cent with ordinary variation of temperature, humidity and barometric pressure. This is larger than the density change produced by a percent-level gas admixture, so any uncompensated density measurement is dominated by the weather rather than by composition.

The drag experienced by a rotating fan depends on bearing friction as well as on gas density. Bearing friction varies from unit to unit and increases with wear. A fan-based measurement that uses only an overall quantity, such as steady speed at fixed drive or total coast-down time, therefore confuses mechanical wear with a change of gas composition.

Conventional automatic mitigation energises an exhaust fan whenever a gas threshold is crossed, irrespective of whether the gas is flammable. It also does not distinguish buoyant from dense gases when selecting the vent path.

3. Prior Patents and Publications from Literature

The search covered Google Patents, the USPTO full-text collection, Espacenet (EPO) records reachable through Google Patents, IEEE Xplore, Crossref and publisher records, standards catalogues (SAE, IEC, IEEE) and manufacturer documentation. The query families were: fan spin-down, coast-down and run-down measurement; estimation of air density from fan or blower operating point; gas-type or gas-family detection from blower behaviour; rotor-damping gas sensors; friction and windage loss separation; temperature and humidity compensation of metal-oxide sensors; multi-sensor gas classification; and automatic gas-leak ventilation. The entries retained are those that bear directly on an element of the present combination.
Method and apparatus for determining fan bearing friction. Dell USA LP.

The closest identified patent on the use of fan spin-down as a measurement. Fan power is interrupted, and the tachometer pulses counted during spin-down (or during spin-up, or the starting voltage) are used as an indicator of bearing friction for failure prediction. Using fan spin-down to track bearing condition is therefore known, and no novelty is asserted for the friction monitor of the present invention taken alone. The reference treats the spin-down rate as a single aggregate quantity governed by rotor inertia and friction. It does not separate speed-independent, viscous and aerodynamic losses, estimate gas density, compensate for temperature, humidity or pressure, or use the result for gas detection.
Fan monitoring for failure prediction. Hewlett-Packard Development Co. LP.

Predicts fan failure from the time derivative of fan power or current at constant speed. Establishes that electrical monitoring of fan load is used for wear detection. No coast-down, no loss-mechanism separation, no gas or density measurement.
Method for detecting the gas family and gas burner. ebm-papst Landshut GmbH (priority 05-09-2012).

The most material reference to the idea that fan behaviour reveals gas composition. In a premix burner, the air mass flow and blower speed are measured before and after fuel gas is admitted, and the change in blower speed identifies the gas family through its effect on the density and flow of the mixture. The reference operates a driven blower at steady state inside a fuel line, with a known fuel deliberately injected and an air-mass meter as reference. It uses no free coast-down, no separation of friction from aerodynamic loss, no thermodynamic reference density derived from ambient temperature, humidity and pressure, and no chemoresistive channel. Its purpose is fuel-family identification for combustion control, not detection and mitigation of an unknown ambient hazard.
Method of controlling a powered air purifying respirator. 3M Innovative Properties Co. (priority 11-08-2009).

Determines ambient air density either from pressure and temperature sensors, or from the fan pressure or speed at a predetermined motor voltage under a known load, and uses it to adjust motor drive and maintain airflow. Both the thermodynamic calculation of air density and the inference of density from a fan operating point are therefore disclosed, albeit as alternatives. The reference does not form the difference between the two to detect a composition change, uses steady powered operation rather than coast-down, does not separate friction, and performs no gas classification.
Furnace control using induced draft blower, exhaust gas flow rate sensing and density compensation. Honeywell Inc.

Recognises that the density of gas passing an induced-draft blower changes blower operation, and compensates the fuel-air ratio using exhaust temperature. Density effects on blower performance are thus long known in combustion control. There is no density measurement from rotor dynamics and no hazard detection.
Temperature and humidity compensation for gas detection apparatus. Standard Oil Company.

Compensates a gas-sensitive semiconductor element for temperature and humidity using a matched gas-insensitive reference element. Environmental compensation of semiconductor gas sensors is old and is not claimed here as such.
Hydrogen sulfide gas detector with humidity and temperature compensation. Rosemount Inc. (priority 29-05-2013).

S sensor for humidity and temperature using co-located or remote humidity and temperature measurements and a compensation equation. The normalisation of the chemoresistive channel against an environment-adjusted reference in the present invention belongs to this known class. No density channel and no hazard classification by gas type.
Gas-leakage emergency protection device. Inventor Huang Xiaohua (application).

A carbon monoxide sensor read by a PLC drives an alarm, a warning lamp and an exhaust fan when a fixed threshold is exceeded. The closest identified art for the sense-decide-ventilate chain. The decision rests on one chemical parameter against one constant. The fan is energised for every detected gas, with no distinction between flammable and inert gases, no choice of vent height and no density information.
Fedchak, J. A., Arai, K., Jousten, K., Setina, J., Yoshida, H.,
Recommended practices for the use of spinning rotor gauges in inter-laboratory comparisons

The most material item of non-patent art on the physical principle. The spinning rotor gauge infers gas density (pressure) from the deceleration of a freely spinning, magnetically levitated rotor, after subtracting a separately determined residual drag that is not caused by the gas. Inferring gas density from rotor deceleration, with correction for non-gas drag, is therefore established metrology, and it is not claimed as new. The gauge works in the molecular-flow vacuum regime with a levitated steel ball. It does not use a bladed fan in continuum-flow air, does not compare its reading with a thermodynamic reference to isolate a composition change, and performs no hazard classification or mitigation.
Absolute pressure and gas species identification with an optically levitated rotor

Shows that the rotational damping of a released, optically levitated microsphere depends on pressure and on gas species, and uses it to identify the gas. This establishes rotor damping as a species-sensitive signal. It is a laboratory vacuum technique with no bearing friction, no ambient-air compensation and no safety application.
Road Load Measurement Using Onboard Anemometry and Coastdown Techniques

Represents vehicle coast-down deceleration by a constant term, a term linear in speed and a term quadratic in speed, and corrects the aerodynamic (quadratic) term for air density. The three-term decomposition of a coast-down into friction and aerodynamic parts by regression is therefore old, and the model form of Equation 3 is acknowledged as known. The standard characterises the vehicle, treating air density as a known correction rather than as the measurand.
US EPA, 40 CFR Part 1066, Subpart D

Regulatory coast-down procedure using the same three-coefficient road-load representation, with correction to reference ambient conditions. Supports the characterisation of Equation 3 as a standard analysis form.
IEEE Standard Test Procedure for Polyphase Induction Motors and Generators

Includes determination of friction and windage losses, and the retardation (deceleration) method is a long-established way of separating mechanical losses in rotating machines. Separation of windage from friction by deceleration is known. The windage term is not used to measure the ambient gas.
Ramachandran, K. P., Rameshkumar, G. R., Al Hatmi, L. H., 2013 IEEE Int. Conf. on Industrial Engineering and Engineering Management (IEEM). DOI 10.1109/IEEM.2013.6962645
Coast Down Time analysis for condition monitoring: an experimental investigation to study the effects of bearing lubrication and shaft misalignment in rotating machinery

Uses coast-down time of a centrifugal blower as a condition-monitoring index for lubrication and misalignment. Confirms that coast-down time is dominated by mechanical condition. This is why an aggregate coast-down time cannot serve as a density signal without friction separation (baseline D of Section 8).
Rameshkumar, G. R., Rao, B. V. A., Ramachandran, K. P.,
Condition Monitoring of Forward Curved Centrifugal Blower Using Coast Down Time Analysis
Earlier coast-down-time study on a blower. As above, the quantity is used for mechanical diagnosis only.
Picard, A., Davis, R. S., Gläser, M., Fujii, K.,
Revised formula for the density of moist air (CIPM-2007)

The metrological reference for the density of humid air as a function of temperature, pressure, humidity and composition. It supplies the basis of the thermodynamic reference density of Equation 8. A formula only, not claimed.
Wang, C., Yin, L., Zhang, L., Xiang, D., Gao, R.,
Metal Oxide Gas Sensors: Sensitivity and Influencing Factors

Reviews the dependence of metal-oxide sensor sensitivity on material, operating temperature and humidity. Establishes the environmental cross-sensitivity that the chemoresistive normalisation must address, and the limited selectivity that motivates a second, physical channel.
Correction Model for Metal Oxide Sensor Drift Caused by Ambient Temperature and Humidity
Regression-based correction of metal-oxide sensor resistance for ambient temperature and humidity. Represents current practice for the normalisation step and is not claimed.
Vergara, A., Vembu, S., Ayhan, T., Ryan, M. A., Homer, M. L., Huerta, R.,
Chemical gas sensor drift compensation using classifier ensembles

Gas discrimination with a 16-element metal-oxide array and trained classifier ensembles. Shows that chemical-only discrimination requires arrays, labelled training data and drift management. The present invention instead obtains an orthogonal physical signal and uses an explicit rule.

Foundational treatment of fusion of dissimilar sensors. The general principle that complementary sensors improve discrimination is known. The reference does not address the specific pairing of an aerodynamic density residual with a chemoresistive response.

on temperature and humidity. Source for the load-resistor measurement arrangement of Equation 12 and for the cross-sensitivity limitation of the chemoresistive channel.

Primary source for the environmental sensor. Specified absolute accuracy is about ±1 °C in temperature, ±3 %RH in relative humidity and ±1 hPa in pressure over the nominal range, which bounds the uncertainty of the thermodynamic reference density. A component specification only.

Documents hardware pulse counting and timer-capture of GPIO edges on the ESP32, which are the on-chip means for per-revolution timing of the tachometer signal. A component specification only.
Explosive atmospheres. Part 10-1: Classification of areas. Explosive gas atmospheres

Establishes that electrical equipment is a potential ignition source in a flammable gas atmosphere and that ventilation and release characteristics, including gas buoyancy, govern hazardous-area extent. Supports the design choice of inhibiting fan energisation and selecting vent height by gas buoyancy. A standard, not claimed.
Stanford Research Systems, BGA244 Binary Gas Analyzer, product documentation
Binary gas analyser based on speed of sound

Commercial determination of the composition of a known binary gas mixture from a physical property (speed of sound) and temperature. Confirms that physical-property gas analysis is established for known binary mixtures in a sampling cell. It does not address unknown ambient admixtures, uses no rotating element and has no chemoresistive channel.
Twin City Fan & Blower, Fan Engineering FE-1600
Temperature and Altitude Effects on Fans
Engineering reference for the fan laws: at fixed speed, fan pressure and absorbed power scale with gas density. Provides the physical basis for the proportionality of the aerodynamic coefficient a

Every entry in Tables 1 and 2 carries a full identifier, which is a patent publication number, a DOI, a journal volume and year, or a standard or document designation. Patent titles, assignees and dates were checked against the Google Patents record of the issuing office. Journal metadata were checked against the Crossref record for the stated DOI. The characterisations of standards and manufacturer documents are limited to their published scope. Formal claim construction of the patent references has not been performed, and an office search by a patent professional is recommended before filing.
4. Summary and Background of the Invention
4.1 Practical Background and Limitations of Existing Solutions

A typical low-cost gas-safety unit consists of a metal-oxide sensor, a microcontroller, a buzzer and a relay that switches an exhaust fan. This arrangement answers one question: whether the resistance of the sensing film has fallen below a threshold. It performs acceptably for the reducing gases the film is designed for, such as liquefied petroleum gas, methane or alcohol vapour. It is blind in three situations that matter in practice. The first is an inert asphyxiant. A carbon dioxide release from a dry-ice store or fire-suppression system, or a helium or nitrogen release from a cylinder, displaces oxygen without changing the film resistance. The second is the distinction between a combustible gas and a harmless solvent or cleaning vapour, both of which lower the resistance, so that the unit is either prone to nuisance alarms or insensitive. The third is buoyancy. Methane rises and accumulates at the ceiling, propane and butane sink and accumulate at floor level, and a unit that knows only the resistance cannot direct ventilation to where the gas is.

The installed mitigation compounds the problem. Switching on an exhaust fan whenever the threshold is crossed is appropriate for a toxic but non-flammable gas. For a combustible gas it introduces an energised electrical device into a potentially flammable mixture, which hazardous-area practice seeks to avoid. The information needed to act correctly is the molecular weight of the contaminant relative to air, which gives heavier or lighter, and whether it is chemically reducing, which gives combustible or not. The first is a physical property that a chemoresistor does not measure.
Gas density does carry that information. At fixed temperature and pressure, admixture of a gas of molar mass M
into air of molar mass M
changes density in proportion to the admixture fraction and to (M

− 1). The difficulty is that the ordinary day-to-day variation of air density, caused by temperature, humidity and barometric pressure, is several per cent, which exceeds the effect of a percent-level leak. Dedicated density meters, including vibrating-element transducers, spinning-rotor gauges and
speed-of-sound analysers, exist, but they are laboratory or process instruments. They are not components of a low-cost ventilation unit.
4.2 Distinctions Over the Closest Reported Systems

The building blocks of this invention are individually known, and the disclosure does not assert otherwise. The inference of gas density from rotor deceleration, with correction for non-gas drag, is the operating principle of the spinning rotor gauge (Fedchak
, 2015). Species-dependent rotor damping has been reported by Blakemore

(2020). The decomposition of a coast-down into constant, linear and quadratic loss terms is standard in vehicle road-load testing (SAE J2263; 40 CFR 1066 Subpart D). The separation of friction and windage by retardation is standard in machine testing (IEEE Std 112). The use of fan spin-down to assess bearing friction is disclosed in US5621159A, and fan-load monitoring for failure prediction in US20060176186A1. The inference of air density from a fan operating point, and its calculation from temperature and pressure, are both disclosed in US9119979B2. Identification of a fuel-gas family from a change of blower speed is disclosed in EP2706300. Temperature and humidity compensation of semiconductor gas sensors is disclosed in US4730479A and US10520481B2, and automatic fan actuation on gas detection in CN102645908A. The distinctions therefore cannot rest on any of those operations. Table 3 maps the feature set against the closest references, and five differences are relied upon.
First, the measurand is the ambient gas and not the machine.

In the road-load, machine-testing and fan-diagnostic art the coast-down characterises the rotating object, with air density treated as a known correction or as a nuisance. Here the rotor is the known quantity, characterised once at commissioning, and the aerodynamic coefficient is used as a transducer output for gas density.
Second, friction is separated and then locked.

US5621159A and the coast-down-time literature use an aggregate spin-down quantity that is dominated by bearing condition. The present method fits the full three-term model to per-revolution timing. It then refits with the viscous coefficient fixed at its commissioning value, so that bearing variation is absorbed by a
and does not leak into a
. Figure 13 and Table 13 show that an aggregate coast-time estimate is displaced by up to about 12 % under added bearing friction, whereas the separated estimate remains within about 0.65 %.
Third, a residual is formed against a thermodynamic reference.

US9119979B2 derives air density either from a fan operating point or from pressure and temperature, and uses whichever it obtains for flow control. It does not compute both and difference them. In the present invention the thermodynamic reference, including humidity, is subtracted from the aerodynamic estimate, so that ordinary weather-driven density change cancels and only composition-driven change remains. The sign of the residual gives the buoyancy of the contaminant.
Fourth, the density residual and the chemoresistive response are fused as two orthogonal axes.
EP2706300 identifies a fuel family from blower speed alone, with a known gas deliberately injected. Chemical-array approaches (Vergara

, 2012) rely on trained classifiers over many chemical channels. Here one physical axis, which responds to molar mass whatever the chemistry, and one chemical axis, which responds to reducing species whatever the mass, are combined by an explicit two-axis rule. The pair separates five classes that neither axis separates alone. These are clean air, inert asphyxiant, buoyant combustible, dense combustible and low-density-effect vapour.
Fifth, mitigation is selected by class and by buoyancy.

CN102645908A energises a fan whenever a gas is detected. Here the fan is driven to full ventilation for an asphyxiant, is left unenergised for a combustible, and the vent path is chosen high for a buoyant combustible and low for a dense one. An

unresolved high chemoresistive response is escalated to the conservative combustible action. The density-channel self-check (friction monitoring and recommissioning) prevents a worn fan from being read as a gas.

The contribution is a cooperative arrangement in which each element conditions the next, not any single operation within it. The per-revolution timing makes the model fit possible. The model fit makes friction separation possible. Friction separation makes the aerodynamic coefficient a density transducer rather than a wear indicator. The thermodynamic reference turns that density into a composition residual. The residual supplies the physical axis on which the chemoresistive response is disambiguated, and the resulting class selects a mitigation that depends on flammability and buoyancy. The friction coefficients produced by the same fit feed back into a self-check that withholds the density axis and recommissions the fan when its mechanics change. Removing any one element either restores the confusion it was introduced to resolve or removes a class from the decision. This is shown by the ablation of Section 8.8, where the omission of thermodynamic compensation, of friction separation, or of the density channel altogether each lowers macro-F1 from 0.759 to between 0.366 and 0.667.

Laboratories and teaching facilities that store compressed gases, dry ice or cryogens are a primary application, because inert asphyxiants are present alongside flammable gases and solvent vapours, and because a single low-cost unit is preferable to separate oxygen, flammable-gas and toxic-gas detectors. Gas-cylinder stores and cabinets benefit from the buoyancy-dependent vent selection. Domestic and commercial kitchens using liquefied petroleum gas or piped natural gas benefit from the distinction between dense and buoyant fuel gases and between fuel gas and cooking vapour. Cold rooms and beverage-dispensing areas using carbon dioxide, battery rooms, small workshops and equipment enclosures that already contain a cooling fan are further applications. In the last case the existing fan can be given a sensing role by adding revolution timing and the processing of Section 7. The unit is constructed from mass-produced components (a microcontroller, a brushless fan with tachometer, a combined temperature, humidity and pressure sensor, and a metal-oxide sensor), so the invention is capable of industrial manufacture.

The primary objective is to provide a single low-cost embedded unit that measures the density of the surrounding gas by means of a fan that the unit also uses for ventilation. The unit compensates that measurement for weather and for mechanical wear, combines it with a chemoresistive measurement to identify the class of gas hazard, and selects a mitigation action appropriate to the flammability and buoyancy of the gas. The specific objectives follow.
To acquire the period of every revolution of a fan during free coast-down after its supply is interrupted, and to derive rotational speed and angular velocity from those periods.

To fit the coast-down record to a rotor-dynamics model that separates speed-independent friction, viscous friction and aerodynamic loss, and to extract an aerodynamic coefficient proportional to gas density.
To stabilise the density estimate against bearing variation by fixing the viscous coefficient at its commissioning value, and by averaging a plurality of coast-downs.

To compute a thermodynamic reference density from the measured temperature, relative humidity and pressure, and to form a signed, standardised density residual that is insensitive to weather and sensitive to composition.

To normalise the chemoresistive response against an environment-adjusted clean-air reference, and to combine it with the density residual in an explicit two-axis classifier that distinguishes clean air, inert asphyxiant, buoyant combustible, dense combustible and low-density-effect vapour.

To select a mitigation action by class, including suppression of fan energisation for combustible gases, choice of a high or low vent path by buoyancy, and conservative escalation of unresolved high chemoresistive responses.

To detect a change of fan mechanics from the friction coefficients, to withhold the density channel while that change is unresolved, and to recommission the calibration automatically from clean-air coast-downs.
To support calibration at more than one fan starting speed, and to record raw and derived quantities so that each decision can be reconstructed afterwards.
6. Working Principle of the Invention (in brief)
The unit executes a measurement cycle in which the fan is used first as a sensor and then, if required, as an actuator. Figure 4 gives the complete sequence and Figure 1 the architecture.
A combined temperature, relative-humidity and pressure sensor (BME280) and an MQ-series metal-oxide sensor are read continuously, typically once per second. The sensing resistance R
of the MQ element is obtained from its load-resistor voltage.

The fan is driven to its operating speed and allowed to stabilise, and then its drive is removed. Each revolution is timed from the tachometer edges. The revolution periods give a record of angular velocity against time from about 2 900 RPM down to about 160 RPM in roughly 18–19 s for the fan characterised in Section 8. The first 0.3 s after cut-off is excluded so that electrical transients of the drive do not enter the fit.
Once the drive is removed, the rotor obeys I dω/dt = −(τ

). The constant term is dry bearing friction, the linear term viscous bearing loss and the quadratic term aerodynamic drag of the blades, which is proportional to gas density ρ. Figure 5(b) shows that the aerodynamic term dominates the deceleration at high speed and friction dominates near rest. The whole coast-down therefore carries separable information on both. The coefficients are obtained by fitting the solution of this equation to the timing record.
With the viscous coefficient locked at its commissioning value, the aerodynamic coefficient a
is averaged over three coast-downs and divided by the commissioning constant K to give the density estimate ρ̂. The thermodynamic reference ρ
is computed from temperature, humidity and pressure, and the residual r = 100(ρ̂/ρ
− 1) and its standardised form z are formed. In clean air z stays near zero. A dense gas drives it positive and a buoyant gas negative.

The pair (z, s) is classified by an explicit rule (Table 8). A negligible chemoresistive response with a significant residual indicates an inert asphyxiant, so the fan is driven at full speed, the vent is opened and an alarm is raised. A significant chemoresistive response with a negative or positive residual indicates a buoyant or dense combustible respectively, so the fan is not energised, the high or low vent path is opened and an alarm is raised. A chemoresistive response

with no significant residual indicates a vapour of small density effect, which leads to partial ventilation and a notification, unless the response is high enough to be escalated to the combustible action.

The friction coefficients from the same fit are compared with their commissioning values. A departure indicating wear withholds the density channel and triggers recommissioning from clean-air coast-downs, after which the viscous lock and the calibration constant are re-established.

The invention comprises a gas-hazard detection and mitigation apparatus built from commercially available components: an axial fan with a tachometer output (101, 102), a supply-voltage monitor (103), a combined temperature, humidity and pressure sensor (104), a metal-oxide chemoresistive sensor (105), a microcontroller hosting the processing and decision layers (200, 300), a fan drive capable of switching and inhibiting the fan (401), a servo-operated vent (402), audible and visual indication (403), a local display (404) and a recording interface (501). What distinguishes it is the manner in which these components act on one another. The fan is both a transducer and an actuator. The friction state of the fan determines whether its transducer output is admitted to the decision. The decision determines not only whether but how the fan and vent are operated, including whether the fan may be energised at all. The output of the apparatus is a set of actuator commands that change the physical state of the protected space.
A mass-produced fan is converted into a gas-density transducer by timing its coast-down, without adding a dedicated density sensor.

Bearing friction, which dominates aggregate coast-down time and varies with wear, is separated from aerodynamic loss by fitting a three-term model, and is kept out of the density estimate by locking the viscous term.

The variation of air density with weather, which is larger than the effect of a percent-level leak, is cancelled by differencing against a thermodynamic reference computed from co-located T, RH and P measurements.

A physical axis that responds to molar mass is paired with a chemical axis that responds to reducing species. This separates inert asphyxiants, which chemoresistors miss, from combustibles, and dense combustibles from buoyant ones.
The mitigation is selected so as not to energise the fan in a combustible atmosphere, and the vent path is chosen by the sign of the density residual.
The same fit that yields density also yields the friction coefficients, which provide a self-check and trigger automatic recommissioning of the density channel.

The invention is embodied as a self-contained unit mounted in the space it protects. The proposed method was experimentally evaluated using the physical hardware implementation described in Section 7 and the breadboard prototype shown in Figure 2. The experimental campaign comprised 256 physical test cases covering clean-air conditions, five admixed gases at multiple concentrations, environmental variations in temperature, relative humidity and pressure, three fan starting speeds, and three levels of bearing friction.

8.4 Gas Sensitivity of the Density Channel
The physical experimental results were analysed to determine the relationship between the measured density residual and gas concentration.
The experimentally measured slopes exhibit the expected signs and approximate magnitudes associated with the molar-mass differences of the tested gases.

The physical results therefore demonstrate that the density residual responds to gas composition through the change in mixture density. Ethanol vapour did not produce a resolvable density residual at the tested concentrations, causing this class to rely primarily on the chemoresistive sensing axis.

Using three standard deviations of the clean-test residual of 0.131% as the detection limit, the density channel experimentally resolved approximately 0.45% vol helium and 0.67% vol carbon dioxide. When the clean-test cases from the wear and speed blocks were also included, the corresponding three-standard-deviation limits increased to approximately 0.99% vol helium and 1.43% vol carbon dioxide.
The effect of environmental variation was evaluated through physical temperature, relative-humidity and pressure sweeps.

Without thermodynamic compensation, the experimentally observed environmental variation produced apparent density changes of up to approximately 4% over the tested ranges. Such variation could mask a percent-level gas-density change or generate a false apparent density event.
After applying the thermodynamic reference, the clean-air density residual remained within the experimentally established ±3σ band throughout the temperature, humidity and pressure sweeps.

The experimentally measured decision latency of the proposed three-coast-down method had a median of 77.23 s, with a range of 55.7–80.1 s.
The latency consists primarily of the three coast-down durations together with a constant processing and control interval of approximately 21.3 s.
For the single-coast-down configuration, the median decision latency was 25.95 s, corresponding to the coast-down duration plus approximately 7.3 s.
The chemoresistive channel responded substantially faster, with a median response time of approximately 4 s.

Consequently, for reducing gases the apparatus can generate a provisional chemoresistive indication within seconds, while the density-dependent classification becomes available following completion of the coast-down sequence.
The measured latency is therefore dominated by the physical coast-down dynamics rather than by computational processing.

Alternative implementations using a lower-inertia fan, shorter fitting window or fewer coast-down cycles could reduce the latency, although the sensitivity-performance trade-off observed in Table 15 would need to be considered.

9.2 Inventive Step of the Claimed Combination

The objection to be met is that every operation in this invention is individually known, and Section 3 concedes this. Gas density from rotor deceleration with non-gas drag subtracted is the spinning rotor gauge. The three-term coast-down is the road-load equation. Friction and windage separation by retardation is in IEEE Std 112. Fan spin-down for bearing friction is in US5621159A. Air density from a fan operating point, or from pressure and temperature, is in US9119979B2. Gas family from blower speed is in EP2706300. Environmental compensation of metal-oxide sensors is in US4730479A and US10520481B2, and fan actuation on gas detection is in CN102645908A. The case for inventive step rests on the cooperative arrangement, and three arguments are advanced.

The first concerns the role reversal of the fan and the residual that makes it work. In every identified coast-down reference the rotating body is the object of measurement and the gas is a known correction. To use a mass-produced ventilation fan as a gas transducer, three obstacles must be overcome together. The friction of a cheap bearing dominates the coast-down (Figure 6). The weather moves air density by more than a leak does. And friction drifts with wear. The three-term fit with viscous lock addresses the first. The thermodynamic residual addresses the second, and it is not suggested by US9119979B2, which treats the two density sources as alternatives. The friction self-check addresses the third. The ablation of Table 15 shows that omitting any one of them removes most of the benefit.

The second concerns the pairing of axes. The prior physical-property analysers (Table 2, entries 1, 2 and 17) measure a known gas or binary mixture. EP2706300 identifies a fuel deliberately injected. None pairs a density residual with a chemoresistive response. That pairing is not a generic fusion of more sensors. It is the specific combination in which each axis resolves the ambiguity of the other: mass without chemistry, and chemistry without mass. It is what allows inert asphyxiants to be detected and buoyant combustibles to be separated from dense ones.

The third concerns the output. The decision selects whether the fan may be energised at all, and at which height the space is vented. These are consequences of the density sign and the chemoresistive response together. No identified reference produces a flammability- and buoyancy-dependent actuation, and CN102645908A, the closest mitigation reference, does the opposite by energising the fan for every detection.
Section 3(k) of the Indian Patents Act, 1970 excludes mathematical methods, algorithms and computer programmes

. The relevant question under current examination practice for computer-related inventions is whether the invention, considered as a whole, solves a technical problem by technical means with a technical effect. The technical problem is that low-cost gas-safety units cannot detect inert asphyxiants or determine gas buoyancy and flammability, and that a fan's coast-down is corrupted by weather and wear. The technical means are physical: a rotating fan whose drive is interrupted, a tachometer, environmental and chemoresistive transducers, and a fan drive, servo vent and alarm. The technical effect is a physical measurement of gas density and the resulting change in the physical state of the protected space, including withholding fan energisation and choosing the vent path. Claims should accordingly be framed as an apparatus and a method of operating it in which the fan is de-energised, its coast-down is timed and processed, and actuators are commanded. The equations belong in the claims as the means by which the sensed state is converted into an actuation decision, not as the subject of the claims.

Section 3(f) excludes the mere arrangement or re-arrangement of known devices each functioning independently in a known way. The parts here do not function independently. The fan is alternately transducer and actuator. The friction state of the fan determines whether its transducer output is admitted. The environmental sensor determines the reference against which the fan output is interpreted. The density sign determines how the chemoresistive response is read, and the resulting class determines whether the fan may be energised. That mutual conditioning is what is put forward as the invention.

The unit requires no trained classifier, no gas-specific calibration of the density channel and no additional density sensor. The calibration constants are obtained by an explicit clean-air commissioning procedure that the unit can repeat by itself.

The main residual limitations are those of Section 8.12: the decision latency is of the order of a minute for three coast-downs, the density resolution does not reach occupational exposure levels, and the behaviour of the sensing spin-up in a flammable atmosphere is to be specified
